topic: Expert C++ Implementation Concept:  Perfect Forwarding and Universal References
explanation: Perfect forwarding efficiently passes arguments to another function, preserving their value categories (lvalue or rvalue).  This is achieved using universal references, which are references that can bind to both lvalues and rvalues. The compiler's implementation relies heavily on template metaprogramming and its understanding of expression categories to achieve this.  Crucially, the compiler uses reference collapsing rules to determine the final type of the forwarded argument, impacting both memory layout and performance.  Rvalue references enable move semantics, significantly impacting performance by avoiding unnecessary copies.  Compile-time behavior involves the generation of specialized function templates based on the argument types, leading to optimized code. Runtime behavior depends on whether the forwarded argument is an lvalue or rvalue, affecting memory management and function call overheads.
syntax: template <typename T> void forwarder(T&& t) { targetFunction(std::forward<T>(t)); }
code_example: forwarder(x); // Forwards lvalue, targetFunction receives lvalue reference
forwarder(std::move(x)); // Forwards rvalue, targetFunction receives rvalue reference
forwarder(10); // Forwards rvalue, targetFunction receives rvalue reference
example_explanation: The `forwarder` function uses a universal reference `T&&`.  When `forwarder` receives an lvalue, `T` deduces to `int&`, and `T&&` collapses to `int&`.  When it receives an rvalue, `T` deduces to `int`, and `T&&` collapses to `int&&`. `std::forward` is crucial; it perfectly forwards the argument's value category, ensuring the correct overload of `targetFunction` is called.  This avoids unnecessary copies when passing rvalues.  The compiler generates different versions of `targetFunction` (or calls existing overloads if they exist and match) based on the deduced types resulting from perfect forwarding.  At runtime, the appropriate version is invoked depending on whether the argument was originally an lvalue or rvalue.  Assembly-level examination would show differing memory access patterns (e.g., direct access versus copying) depending on the argument category.
